[Runtime support](../README.md#runtime-support)

Import functions by name from the package root. Function subpaths support default and named ES module imports; CommonJS subpaths return the function directly. Root and subpath imports refer to the same functions. See the [import examples](../README.md#usage).

## Object defaults

### `withDefaults(defaults?, ...overrides)`

Performs a shallow merge of defaults and overrides into a new object, preserving earlier values when a property is missing or `undefined`.

Use it to supply default values without writing a separate fallback for each property. Pass defaults first, then override objects from left to right. A later defined value replaces the earlier value, including when it is `null`, `false`, `0` or an empty string. An `undefined` override keeps the most recent earlier value.

**Parameters**

| Parameter      | Type                              | Description                                                |
| -------------- | --------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `defaults?`    | `object \| null \| undefined`     | Optional object containing the initial default values.     |
| `...overrides` | `(object \| null \| undefined)[]` | Zero or more override objects, applied from left to right. |

Arguments that are `null` or `undefined` are skipped in any position. With no arguments, the result is an empty object. Functions and other non-object arguments are rejected; function-valued properties are valid.

**Returns:** `Object` — A new plain object containing the combined properties. Nested objects and arrays retain their original references.

**Errors**

- `TypeError` if an argument is not an object, `null` or `undefined`. Rejected arguments are not coerced or invoked.
- Getter, proxy and reflection errors are passed through to the caller. Arguments are processed in order; after an error, later arguments are not read and earlier getter side effects are not undone.

**Examples**

Supply defaults for an `undefined` title while preserving explicit `false` and `0` values:

<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```javascript
const { withDefaults } = require('go-defaults');

const defaults = { title: 'Home', visible: true, count: 10 };
const overrides = { title: undefined, visible: false, count: 0 };

withDefaults(defaults, overrides);   // => { title: 'Home', visible: false, count: 0 }
```

An `undefined` override keeps the most recent value, so it does not reset `count` to `10`:

<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```javascript
const { withDefaults } = require('go-defaults');

const defaults = { count: 10 };
const firstOverride = { count: 4 };
const lastOverride = { count: undefined };

withDefaults(defaults, firstOverride, lastOverride);   // => { count: 4 }
```

Without any defined properties to copy, the result is empty. Properties containing only `undefined` are omitted:

<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```javascript
const { withDefaults } = require('go-defaults');

withDefaults();                      // => {}
withDefaults(null, undefined);       // => {}
withDefaults({ title: undefined });  // => {}
```

**Notes**

#### Shallow copying

A nested override replaces the whole nested value. Its properties are not merged with those of the default, and neither object is cloned:

<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```javascript
const { withDefaults } = require('go-defaults');

const defaults = { appearance: { colour: 'blue', size: 'large' } };
const overrides = { appearance: { colour: 'red' } };
const result = withDefaults(defaults, overrides);

result;                                      // => { appearance: { colour: 'red' } }
result.appearance === overrides.appearance;  // => true
defaults.appearance;                         // => { colour: 'blue', size: 'large' }
```

#### Property copying

Only **own enumerable string and symbol properties** are copied. Inherited and non-enumerable properties are skipped. Symbols follow the same override rule:

<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```javascript
const { withDefaults } = require('go-defaults');

const label = Symbol('label');
const defaults = { [label]: 'Home' };
const result = withDefaults(defaults, { [label]: undefined });

result[label];                 // => 'Home'
```

For each source, the helper takes a snapshot of its own keys, then checks each property's current enumerability before reading it. Each eligible value is read once. A getter's defined return value becomes an ordinary writable, configurable, enumerable data property in the result; the getter itself is not copied. Getters and proxies can have side effects even though the helper does not assign to its sources.

Special names such as `__proto__` become own data properties without invoking inherited setters or changing the result's prototype:

<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```javascript
const { withDefaults } = require('go-defaults');

const source = JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"unexpected":true}}');
const result = withDefaults(source);

Object.getPrototypeOf(result) === Object.prototype;          // => true
Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(result, '__proto__');   // => true
result.unexpected;                                           // => undefined
```

This protects the copying operation. The result can still contain values that are unsafe for a later operation, including another merge that handles `__proto__` differently.

#### Other object types

Plain data objects are the usual inputs. Other objects follow the same property-copying rules: arrays contribute enumerable indices, excluding `length`; class instances contribute own enumerable fields, excluding prototype methods. `Map` and `Set` entries and a `Date`'s stored time are not enumerable properties, so they are not extracted. Any extra own enumerable properties on those objects are still eligible.

Pass an object as an argument, even when its properties contain primitive values:

<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```javascript
const { withDefaults } = require('go-defaults');

withDefaults({}, { count: 0 });  // => { count: 0 }
withDefaults({}, 123);           // => throws TypeError
```

#### Comparison with JavaScript defaults

The fallback rule matches JavaScript [default parameters](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Functions/Default_parameters) and [destructuring defaults](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Destructuring#default_value): only `undefined` uses an earlier value. The evaluation timing differs. JavaScript default expressions run only when needed. Objects passed to [`withDefaults`](#withdefaultsdefaults-overrides) have already been evaluated, and the helper reads their eligible properties in argument order.

### `createDefaultsMerger(options?)`

Creates a reusable function that merges objects with your defaults rules.

Pass defaults followed by overrides each time you call the returned function. Omit the options for the same shallow behavior as [`withDefaults`](#withdefaultsdefaults-overrides). Set `shouldFallback` to keep earlier values for other inputs, or set `mergeDepth` to combine matching nested records.

**Parameters**

| Parameter                | Type                                                 | Description                                                                       |
| ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `options`                | `object`                                             | Optional configuration. The factory captures the individual settings when called. |
| `options.shouldFallback` | `(value: unknown, key: string \| symbol) => boolean` | Optional rule. Defaults to `value => value === undefined`.                        |
| `options.mergeDepth`     | `number`                                             | Optional nonnegative safe integer. Defaults to `0`.                               |

**Returns:** `Function` — `(defaults?, ...overrides) => Object` — A reusable function that returns a fresh plain object.

**Errors**

- `TypeError` for invalid options, a nonnumeric depth, or a supplied predicate that is not a function.
- `RangeError` if the depth is negative, fractional, nonfinite or outside the safe integer range.
- `TypeError` if the predicate returns anything other than a primitive boolean, including a promise.
- Errors from the predicate, getters and reflection propagate. Source layers follow the [input rules of `withDefaults`](#withdefaultsdefaults-overrides).

**Examples**

Reuse a rule that treats `null` and `undefined` as unanswered fields. The last override keeps the title supplied by the preceding override.

<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```javascript
import { createDefaultsMerger } from 'go-defaults';

const mergeForm = createDefaultsMerger({
  shouldFallback: value => value === undefined || value === null
});
mergeForm({ title: 'Home' }, { title: 'Guide' }, { title: null, subtitle: null });  // => { title: 'Guide' }
mergeForm({ title: 'Contact' }, { title: null });  // => { title: 'Contact' }
```

Merge `params` one level below the root, keeping its earlier `bar` value.

<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```javascript
import createDefaultsMerger from 'go-defaults/createDefaultsMerger';

const merge = createDefaultsMerger({ mergeDepth: 1 });
const page = merge({ title: 'Home', params: { foo: 1, bar: 2 } }, { params: { foo: 'new' } });
page;  // => { title: 'Home', params: { foo: 'new', bar: 2 } }
```

#### Fallback rule

A supplied predicate replaces the built-in rule. It receives each visited own enumerable override value once, including an explicit `undefined`. Initial defaults at the root bypass the predicate and only their defined values are copied. A `true` result keeps the most recent earlier own value, or leaves the property absent if there is none. A `false` result accepts the override. Numeric property names arrive as strings, and symbol keys retain their identity.

#### Nested record behavior

- Depth counts levels below the root. At depth `0`, an accepted nested value replaces the earlier value as a whole. Depth `1` can merge records directly inside the root, and depth `2` can also merge records inside those records.
- A nested merge needs two records for the same own property. An eligible value is a non-null, non-array object with an immediate prototype of `null` or the current realm’s `Object.prototype`. Arrays, ordinary class instances, native collections and foreign-realm object literals remain whole values. A proxy follows the prototype it reports.
- The merger visits layers left to right and nested records depth-first. It reads each eligible incoming value before calling the predicate, then decides whether to descend. If the earlier record came from an input, the merger copies its own enumerable entries before reading the incoming record’s entries. Earlier own `undefined` values are preserved when an override falls back.
- A first-seen branch, a branch replacing a non-record, or a branch at the depth limit is taken by reference. Its child properties go unvisited. Defaults-only branches also keep their references.
- A merged branch is a fresh ordinary object. Later overrides can update that object within the same call. Merges write own data properties safely, including `__proto__`, and finite depth bounds traversal through cycles. A retained branch can still share references with an input or contain a cycle. Shared branches merged in separate places can produce separate objects.

## Single-value defaults

### `defaultIf(value, fallback, predicate?)`

Returns a fallback if a value meets a condition.

Use it to choose between two values in an expression. The built-in condition matches only `undefined`. Supply a predicate when another value, such as `null` or an empty string, should trigger fallback.

**Parameters**

| Parameter    | Type                 | Description                                                                   |
| ------------ | -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `value`      | `any`                | Required value to test.                                                       |
| `fallback`   | `any`                | Required value to return when the test passes. Explicit `undefined` is valid. |
| `predicate?` | `(value) => boolean` | Optional replacement test. Defaults to `value => value === undefined`.        |

**Returns:** `any` — The fallback when the predicate returns `true`. Otherwise, the supplied value. References are preserved.

**Errors**

- `TypeError` if either value argument is omitted or a supplied predicate is invalid.
- `TypeError` if the predicate returns anything other than a primitive boolean, including a promise.
- Exceptions thrown by the predicate propagate to the caller.

**Examples**

Use the built-in rule to preserve explicit values.

<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```javascript
const { defaultIf } = require('go-defaults');

defaultIf(undefined, 'Home');  // => 'Home'
defaultIf(null, 'Home');       // => null
defaultIf(false, true);        // => false
defaultIf(0, 10);              // => 0
```

Supply a predicate when only `null` should trigger fallback.

<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```javascript
import { defaultIf } from 'go-defaults';

const isNull = value => value === null;
defaultIf(null, 'Home', isNull);       // => 'Home'
defaultIf(undefined, 'Home', isNull);  // => undefined
```

Use [`withDefaults`](#withdefaultsdefaults-overrides) to apply defaults to individual properties of an object.

<!-- prettier-ignore -->
```javascript
const { defaultIf, withDefaults } = require('go-defaults');

const defaults = { title: 'Home' };
const supplied = {};

defaultIf(supplied, defaults) === supplied;  // => true
withDefaults(defaults, supplied);              // => { title: 'Home' }
```

**Notes**

Arguments are evaluated before the call, starting with `value`. The predicate receives that value once. Objects, arrays, functions and promises are returned by reference. To evaluate an expensive fallback only when needed, use a conditional expression.

## TypeScript

### Single-value inference

[`defaultIf`](#defaultifvalue-fallback-predicate) preserves the supplied value’s type when the built-in rule can rule out `undefined`. When the supplied type includes `undefined`, the result includes the fallback’s type. A custom predicate can select either argument, so the result includes both types.

```typescript
import { defaultIf } from 'go-defaults';

function readCount(value: number | undefined): number {
  return defaultIf(value, 10);
}

const title: string = defaultIf(undefined, 'Home');
const explicitNull: null = defaultIf(null, 10);
// defaultIf(undefined); // TypeScript error: the fallback argument is required.
```

The same signatures apply to root and focused imports. Known-defined generic values retain their type even when the default has a broad type. Objects, readonly tuples, function signatures and promise types are preserved without applying object-merge inference.

### Property inference

For ordinary objects with known properties, TypeScript infers the result from the defaults and overrides. With the built-in rule, a defined override supplies the new property type and an `undefined` override keeps the earlier type.

```typescript
import { withDefaults, createDefaultsMerger } from 'go-defaults';

const preserved = withDefaults({ count: 10 }, { count: undefined });
const count: number = preserved.count;

const replaced = withDefaults({ count: 10 }, { count: 'many' });
const description: string = replaced.count;

const merge = createDefaultsMerger();
const cleared = merge({ visible: true }, { visible: null });
const visible: null = cleared.visible;
```

Inference accounts for shallow replacement, `undefined` fallback, optional properties, arguments that may be `null` or `undefined`, symbol keys and a fresh mutable result. Literal types supplied with `as const` stay literal types. Properties whose only possible value is `undefined` are omitted.

Numeric keys use their JavaScript string spelling, so `1` and `'1'` refer to the same property:

```typescript
import { withDefaults } from 'go-defaults';

const result = withDefaults({ 1: 'first' }, { '1': 'second' });
const byNumber: string = result[1];
const byString: string = result['1'];
```

Each property's type is calculated separately, working back from the last override until a guaranteed value is found. This avoids expanding every combination of whole-object unions, but it does not preserve relationships between different properties in a union. Narrow the source to the relevant union branch first when you need that relationship.

### When result properties are unknown

Precise inference supports tuples of up to **64 source objects**, including the defaults argument passed to a merger created by [`createDefaultsMerger`](#createdefaultsmergeroptions). Larger tuples, optional or unbounded source spreads, dictionaries with index signatures, arrays and opaque `object` inputs produce a result with unknown-valued properties. This limit affects type precision; the runtime accepts any number of source objects. Complex property types remain subject to the compiler's own limits.

In a conservative result, built-in property names such as `toString`, `valueOf` and `constructor` are explicitly `unknown` too: an input may replace them with a non-function. Template-pattern index signatures, even when combined with fixed keys, use the same dictionary fallback. Finite template expansions retain their known keys.

Known native instance types, including `Date`, `Map`, `Set`, `RegExp`, primitive wrappers, promises and binary-buffer views, also produce conservative results. Their typed methods are generally inherited and are not copied, but instances can have extra own enumerable properties. Neither the full instance type nor an empty result type would describe that reliably.

TypeScript checks structure, so an ordinary object shaped like a native wrapper—for example, one with only `valueOf(): boolean`—can also receive a conservative result. The native-type checks do not require newer ambient library definitions merely to import the package.

### Ownership and inherited properties

TypeScript does not track property ownership or enumerability. Precise inference for records assumes their visible fields are own enumerable data. For custom classes, `Error` objects, browser host objects or unusual property descriptors, widen the source to `object` to request conservative typing. This changes the inferred type, not the runtime copying rules.

Optional fields that shadow `Object.prototype` methods include the inherited fallback in their result type. For example, `{ toString?: string }` can leave either an own string or the inherited `toString` function. With the built-in rule, a guaranteed defined override retains its exact type. Host-dependent legacy prototype names such as `__proto__` remain `unknown` when every source may skip them.

### Inputs and generic wrappers

For object merging, the declarations reject known primitive layers, including branded scalar types, and function or constructor arguments. Invalid branches in unions, optional tuples and spread arrays are rejected too. Property values may be any type, including functions and branded primitives. Broad `object` and `any` types can hide invalid arguments, so runtime validation still applies.

An unresolved generic such as `Layer extends object` can include a function intersection, even with a dictionary constraint. Passing it directly can therefore fail type checking. If a wrapper deliberately leaves validation to runtime, widen that argument to `object` and accept the conservative result type. Concrete records with generic property values retain inference; their function-valued properties remain valid.

### Inference with a custom rule

With a custom `shouldFallback` rule, [`createDefaultsMerger`](#createdefaultsmergeroptions) includes earlier and later possible property types. This includes `undefined` when an override can explicitly supply it. For ordinary records, a property with a definite default remains required. A property introduced only by overrides is optional.

When `mergeDepth` is positive or may be positive, known root keys keep their presence and scalar types, including branded strings and numbers. TypeScript gives root properties that may contain objects the type `unknown` because it cannot tell which records will merge or what shape the result will have.

An options type can hide settings when its properties are optional or absent. The return type accounts for a custom rule unless the options type establishes `shouldFallback: undefined`. It allows for nested merging unless the type establishes `mergeDepth: 0` or `mergeDepth: undefined`. Omit the options entirely for the same inference as `withDefaults`.

### Compiler support

Use **TypeScript 4.5.2 or later**. The minimum applies to the compiler that checks your code, while the [runtime requirements](../README.md#runtime-support) apply to the JavaScript you run. A newer compiler can produce CommonJS code for Node.js 8; the compiler itself does not have to run on Node.js 8.

| Module resolution                                        | Minimum TypeScript version |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| Traditional Node resolution (`moduleResolution: "node"`) | 4.5.2                      |
| Node16 / NodeNext                                        | 4.7.2                      |
| Bundler                                                  | 5.0.2                      |

Named imports from function subpaths require Node16, NodeNext or Bundler resolution. With legacy `node` resolution, use named root imports or default subpath imports. Default subpath imports need `esModuleInterop` for CommonJS output, or `allowSyntheticDefaultImports` for ES module output.

All three use the same inference and input-validation contracts. The package includes generated `.d.ts` declarations for older resolution modes and `.d.cts` / `.d.mts` declarations for modern CommonJS and ESM resolution.

TypeScript 4.4 and earlier are unsupported: the existing large-tuple inference cases exceed their type-recursion limits. Supporting them would require changing the declaration strategy or reducing the supported precision. The minimum preserves inference for up to 64 sources, `undefined` fallbacks, symbol and numeric keys, and rejection of known invalid inputs.

The compiler matrix checks 4.5.2, 4.7.2, 5.0.2, 5.4.5 and the pinned 6.0.3 compiler against an installed package. It checks supported resolution modes, optional-property settings and emitted consumers. This is a tested matrix, not a claim that every compiler patch has been run. The [development section](../README.md#development) lists the separate contributor tool requirements.
